description: Deep-cut assumptions, prosperity slogans, and subtle errors designed to challenge mature players.

items.saying: The Bible says ‘God will not give you more than you can handle’
items.explanation: This slogan merges parts of Paul's teaching into a phrase the Bible never actually uses. Paul speaks of God providing a way of escape in temptation (1 Corinthians 10:13), but he also boasts in situations that are far beyond his own ability so that Christ's power may rest on him (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

items.saying: The safest place in the world is the center of God's will
items.explanation: In Acts 21, Paul is warned that chains and affliction await him, yet he is resolved to do God's will. Obedience did not lead him away from danger but into it. The cliché oversimplifies God's providence and can mislead believers about the cost of discipleship.

items.saying: If you have enough faith, you will always be healed
items.explanation: Scripture records instances of miraculous healing, yet it also shows faithful believers who are not healed in this life. Paul's thorn in the flesh remained despite his prayers (2 Corinthians 12:7–9), and Timothy is advised to take wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23). The idea that healing is guaranteed by sufficient faith goes beyond Scripture.

items.saying: If you speak it, you can create your reality
items.explanation: God creates reality by His word (Hebrews 11:3), but humans do not share that divine power in the same way. Proverbs 18:21 teaches that the tongue has power in its effects on people and situations, not that humans can unconditionally create realities by speech. The slogan confuses God's unique creative word with human confession.

items.saying: God will never violate your free will
items.explanation: The Bible never states this rule. God can restrain, redirect, or overpower human intentions, as in His warning to Abimelech in Genesis 20:3–6 or Christ's confrontation of Saul in Acts 9:1–6. Scripture holds together both human responsibility and God's sovereign intervention.

items.saying: If you just believe hard enough, God must answer your prayer
items.explanation: This saying, 'If you just believe hard enough, God must answer your prayer', is a common way of thinking in some church or cultural settings, but it is not a Bible verse and often distorts biblical teaching. Scripture presents a more balanced view: God's sovereignty does not cancel human responsibility; faith does not guarantee earthly comfort; and outward success or emotion is not a reliable measure of God's favor. Believers are called to test such ideas against the whole counsel of Scripture rather than accepting them as automatic spiritual laws.

Feelings and results must be tested by the Word of God, not treated as infallible indicators of His will.
